entities.summary:
The Borjgali, an emblematic symbol of the sun and eternity, is integral to Georgian cultural identity, emerging during the classical era as a representation of life's cyclical nature and the interconnectedness of existence. Its distinctive design features seven wings radiating from a central point, often depicted above the tree of life, symbolizing harmony and the eternal cycle of life and death. This iconography not only reflects the spiritual beliefs of the ancient Georgians but also illustrates the broader themes of nature worship that permeated various ancient cultures across the globe.

The creation of the Borjgali can be traced back to the early periods of Georgian history, with its roots possibly extending to the 4th century BCE, during which it was utilized in various religious and cultural practices. The symbol’s presence in Georgian architecture, textiles, and art has been well-documented, particularly in the medieval period, where it adorned churches and manuscripts, signifying its importance in both religious and everyday life. During the Soviet era, the Borjgali was revived as a national symbol, reflecting the resilience of Georgian culture amidst external influences and conflicts.

As a cultural artifact, the Borjgali has left an enduring legacy, influencing contemporary Georgian nationalism and serving as an emblem of identity for the Georgian diaspora worldwide. Its representation in modern art and architecture underlines the continuing relevance of this ancient symbol, connecting present-day Georgians with their historical roots. The Borjgali symbolizes not just a heritage but a living connection to the traditions and values of the Georgian people, illustrating how symbols can transcend time and continue to resonate in modern contexts.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Borjgali (Georgian: ბორჯღალი, Borjghali) is an ancient Georgian symbol — a seven-armed rotating sun wheel or solar disc, composed of seven curved or hooked arms radiating from a central point in a pinwheel/swastika-like rotating pattern — that has been a symbol of the sun, eternal motion, and the cycle of life in Georgian culture from ancient times. The symbol is found in Georgian church architecture (particularly in the carved stone reliefs of medieval Georgian churches such as the Jvari Monastery, 6th century, and the Svetitskhoveli Cathedral, 11th century), in medieval manuscripts, in Georgian folk art (textiles, jewellery, ceramics), and in archaeological artefacts from the Bronze Age cultures of the Caucasus. The Borjgali is one of the most distinctive symbols in Georgian cultural tradition — its seven-armed form (seven being a sacred number in Georgian cosmology and Christian symbolism) distinguishes it from other solar wheel symbols found across Eurasia.

The Borjgali appears most prominently in the context of Georgian Orthodox Christianity — the Church of Georgia adopted the symbol as a decorative element in its sacred architecture, integrating the pre-Christian solar symbolism with Christian theological content (Christ as the 'Sun of Righteousness', the eternal motion of divine providence). The symbol's appearance in the Jvari Monastery — one of the earliest surviving examples of Georgian sacred architecture and a UNESCO World Heritage Site — and in the carved stonework of the Svetitskhoveli Cathedral (the primary cathedral of Georgia, seat of the Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia) gives it its primary association with the Georgian Orthodox Church and Georgian national identity.

The Borjgali has been revived as a major symbol of Georgian national identity in the post-Soviet period (since 1991) — appearing on jewellery, clothing, tattoos, and official representations of Georgian cultural heritage.
